turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Brendan, you're next. Blood pressure is 146 over 88, pulse 76, both grand. I've the repeat list from the chemist here.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): In you come. Repeat prescriptions today, is it?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It is, yeah, and um, I want something stronger for this knee while I'm at it. It's giving me awful gyp.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which knee?

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): The right. Same knee as always, five years or six, I couldn't tell you when it started. We were down the town yesterday, the bus was late, and the butcher had no rashers, but that's another day's work.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, the right knee's been worse for three weeks. He's given up the evening walks and he won't admit it.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks, not three. It's awful when I walk, eases if I sit a minute. She's timing me like a hawk.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nurse, the co-codamol on that list, what dose?
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Pharmacy list says co-codamol 30/500, two tablets four times a day.
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): That's not right. Well, actually, my box is the 8/500, two in the morning and two at teatime. I never take four lots.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the naproxen?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Naproxen 500 milligrams, one in the morning and one at night, by mouth, for the knee. That one on the list is right.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The night tablet is often still in the dosette box. He skips it, half the evenings I'd say.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): I take it when I remember. Mostly I do. Don't be telling him I don't.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any stomach trouble with the naproxen?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Stomach's grand, not a bother.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the knee, or does it give way?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No swelling, and it doesn't give way.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain.
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He goes dizzy when he stands up out of the chair. I've seen him grab the table.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): I am not dizzy. The once, the kettle was boiling and I got up quick. She's making a meal of it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not prescribing anything stronger. No tramadol, and no morphine.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah, even a short go of it? Yer man next door is on tramadol and he says it's mighty. They offered me tramadol once and I never took it, never collected the script.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Still no. Are you still taking the amitriptyline?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Stopped that in March. Ten milligrams at night. It had me groggy of a morning, so I left it off, and I haven't taken one since.
[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He did sleep a bit better when he was on it, I'll give it that.

[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Sleep is fine, leave it. Actually, I said the stomach was grand, but the naproxen does give me a burn, heartburn, up in the chest about an hour after I take it. A glass of milk settles it.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heartburn after the naproxen, settled with milk. Take it with food. I'm not starting a stomach tablet today.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand. The chemist was shut Monday on account of the match, and the queue was a holy show. Not your worry.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me see that knee. Bend it for me.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): No heat in it, no swelling I can feel. There is crepitus when you bend it.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the grinding, yeah. My father had the same, ended up with two new knees. I'm not looking for an operation, God no.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd call this your osteoarthritis flaring. I wouldn't put another name on it without the bloods.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): The arthritis, yeah, that's what they called it. It's been there years.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll order a kidney blood test and a full blood count, on account of the naproxen.
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): I can do the bloods this morning. There's a slot in about ten minutes.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it's no better in six weeks we might x-ray the knee. Not today.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks is a fair stretch if I'm hobbling. I drove the buses, retired ten years, and it was always this leg on the clutch. I'm rambling, sorry.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks. If the knee locks or you can't walk on it, come sooner.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): And which co-codamol am I supposed to be swallowing?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't change anything. I can't tell if you're on the 8 or the 30 until I see the box. Bring the packet next time.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): It's in the press, behind the porridge. Myself and my daughter Aoife live together, and she keeps that press like a barracks.
[SEG0046] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the box in, so.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Naproxen stays 500 milligrams twice a day, with food. I'll reissue that repeat today.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): And nothing stronger. You're sure now.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing stronger. Don't buy extra paracetamol either. It's already in the co-codamol.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, I won't so. I had a mind to pick a box up in the chemist. Good job you said.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): Bloods in ten minutes. I'll call you from the corridor.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Sound. I'll nip to the toilet first, too much tea, nothing medical. Thanks, doctor.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Doctor planned tests; 'in about ten minutes' was nurse's blood draw timing, not doctor's action time.
bad.text: Kidney blood test and full blood count (action_type=investigation, status=planned, responsible_person=doctor, time_reference=value: in about ten minutes)

omissions.text: Co-codamol details are incomplete: patient said his box is co-codamol 8/500 and he takes 2 tablets in the morning and 2 at teatime; he explicitly said he never takes 2 tablets four times a day as on the pharmacy list.
Amitriptyline was stopped in March because it made him groggy in the morning, and he has not taken any since.
Patient initially denied stomach trouble from naproxen before later clarifying heartburn/burning in the chest about an hour after taking it.
Doctor said he was not starting a stomach tablet today despite naproxen-related heartburn.
Doctor said he would not put another name on the knee problem without blood tests.
Nurse offered to do the kidney blood test and full blood count that morning, with a slot in about 10 minutes.
